title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short position-style essays produced for the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it asks how AI education should evolve in three broad areas: integrating ethics throughout AI curricula, teaching AI to secondary school and early undergraduate students, and making AI education more interdisciplinary so that non-engineering students can benefit from it.

Across the contributions, the authors propose a range of pedagogical approaches. These include peer-learning seminars and interdisciplinary projects, more student-centric discovery learning inspired by Montessori principles, concrete early-introduction activities using games and puzzles, real-world problem-based instruction, and active-learning formats for teaching AI concepts with high-school-level mathematics. Several essays also argue that ethics should not be a separate topic but should be embedded across search, planning, knowledge representation, machine learning, robotics, and project-based courses.

The intended populations are secondary school students, undergraduate students, and early-career educators, with contexts spanning classrooms, labs, and blended learning environments. Because the paper is conceptual and forward-looking, it does not test whether any of the proposed approaches improve outcomes relative to standard instruction. Its main conclusion is that AI education should become more interdisciplinary, more experiential, and more ethically grounded, especially if the field wants to broaden participation and prepare students for real-world AI practice.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a collection of opinion/position essays from a symposium and does not present a formal study design, sample, comparison group, or quantitative evaluation. It is useful as conceptual/adjacent evidence but not as empirical evidence of intervention effects.
impact_tier_rationale: No measured impact is reported, so there is no evidence of positive or negative effect sizes for K-12 scientific reasoning or inquiry. The paper is best treated as descriptive background and design speculation rather than impact evidence.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual AI and programming instruction through game- and simulation-like classroom activities, including using the General Video Game AI framework, card/map-based A* search demonstrations, and agent-based models in puzzles/games for secondary-school learners.

Non-traditional instructional delivery of AI concepts through short instructor introductions, group activities, videos, books, and software-supported exploration rather than conventional lecture-based teaching.

finding.finding_summary: This is a blue-sky, conceptual symposium paper rather than an empirical study, so it does not report outcome data, effect sizes, or comparative results. Across the essays, the intended scientific-reasoning benefit is to help secondary-school learners understand AI concepts such as search, planning, and machine learning through hands-on activities, real-world problems, and interdisciplinary projects.

The paper argues that these instructional approaches are meant to build critical thinking, reasoning, collaboration, and informed choice-making, but it presents no empirical evaluation. For example, peer-learning seminars, project-based interdisciplinary work, and student-centric discovery are proposed as ways to strengthen independent thinking and teamwork in AI education.
